candidates.raw_excerpt: Varda has closed a $251M Series D to scale its business of making pharmaceuticals in orbit. Lux Capital and Natural Capital led the round, which valued the company at $1.6B. Founders Fund, Khosla Ventures, Caffeinated Capital, General Catalyst, 8090 Industries, Giant Step, and Also Capital also joined. The new funding brings the total amount raised by Varda to nearly $600M. Zero-G benefits: Space offers significant benefits for pharmaceutical manufacturing, since the lack of gravity allows medical ingredients to crystallize together in ways that would be impossible on Earth, creating new and more effective medicines.  However, Varda’s capsules are also used by semiconductor manufacturers, who reap similar benefits in low gravity, and national security customers looking to test out tech at hypersonic re-entry speeds. Waiting to fly: Since 2023, Varda has flown six re-entry missions, with more than a dozen more planned over the next two years.  Two of those are expected to get a taste of space in fairly short order, with the company’s W-8 and W-9 missions set to launch aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 as soon as Thursday. W-8 will carry sensors to study the capsule’s temperature and other data during re-entry, and includes thermal protection materials on the outside under a US military study. W-9 includes a DoD payload to test navigation during hypersonic flight. The outside will test advanced heat shield tiles from Syensqo. Their study, published in the research journal Joule , outlines a new type of solar panel built with perovskites — a calcium titanium oxide mineral — instead of silicon. By using pervoskite-based cells, the researchers were able to adjust the solar panels to capitalize on the kinds of blue and green sunlight waves that can penetrate the ocean’s surface. According to the paper, the peak power conversion efficiency — a measure of how much sunlight hitting a panel is converted into usable energy — reached a high of nearly 35 percent. If true, that figure puts the panels in-line with recent breakthrough research in solar cell efficiency, and a notch above the long-established Shockley-Queisser limit , a theoretical cap which limited photovoltaic efficiency to about 33 percent. Granted, the results were obtained under simulation conditions, so more rigorous testing is needed to confirm whether similar results are possible in a real-world setting. Overall, the test ran for just two hours, generating 324 milliwatt-hours, enough to power a small LED light for a few hours. Still, even sniffing the Shockley-Queisser limit with solar panels some 30 feet underwater is a noteworthy accomplishment. And as EuroNews observes, even the decidedly small amount of electricity produced far surpassed researchers’ expectations. candidates.title: CNES Publishes Call for New Rocket Launch Tracking Turrets for French Guiana
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: CSG The French space agency CNES has issued a call for new automated optical tracking systems for the Guiana Space Centre. The new system will need to be capable of tracking launch vehicles to altitudes of up to an altitude of 100 kilometres. Published on 24 September , the initiative aims to replace aging and partially obsolete equipment currently used to capture imagery of Ariane and Vega launches. CNES said the existing systems are ageing and partially obsolete. The agency wants to replace the manual and semi-automated systems with a fully automated alternative, with tracking tied directly to launch vehicle trajectory data. Beyond launch imagery for public broadcasts, the spaceport’s flight-safety teams use these systems for technical analysis and diagnostics to support post-launch investigations. The new tracking turrets will carry sensors operating in both the visible and infrared spectrum, together with very-long-focal-length optics capable of clearly observing a launch vehicle at an altitude of 100 kilometres. In total, CNES plans to procure three turrets. Two will be fixed systems, while the third will be a mobile unit that can be positioned where it’s needed. CNES will install one fixed turret on Île Royale, an island off the coast of French Guiana, and the second on the mainland. The turrets will be managed remotely and operated from a single console at the Image Production Centre (Centre de Production d’Images) in the Jupiter 2 building, which is also home to the spaceport’s main control centre. CNES expects to award the contract in the third quarter of 2027. The contract, covering the supply, installation and qualification of the new systems, is expected to run for approximately three years. candidates.title: Creative Industries Have Been Eviscerated by AI, Data Shows
candidates.raw_excerpt: If you work in a creative industry or media, you probably don’t need anybody to tell you how bad things have gotten. Still, even the most intimate first-hand knowledge can’t prepare you for the sheer scope of the devastation. As data journalist Joseph Politano found in a new Substack post , the US has lost more than 200,000 jobs in “creative” industries over the past four years — the period since the first version of ChatGPT became available to the public — with almost 50,000 of those losses coming in the last year alone. The data comes from the US Bureau of Labor statistics, the trustworthiness of which has been repeatedly undermined since Donald Trump’s return to office. Still, it remains one of the most robust and widely-used indicators of macroeconomic job data, for analysts trying to make sense of the increasingly bleak job market . “That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” Politano observes, “with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008.” Politano notes the steepest losses came in digital arts like graphic design, broadcasting, publishing, as well as films and sound recording. Though some sections of the live arts sector have actually grown precipitously — museum work and performing arts, to be precise — other types of live arts jobs, like “employment to an independent artist” have plummeted compared to years past. As a whole, job growth in media and creative industries has remained negative since 2023, as tools like generative AI — shoddy as they still are — provide an easily accessible alternative to human design, video, literary, and audio work. Though it’s never been easy to secure consistent employment in these industries, the rise of AI and the general decay of the labor economy has clearly made it harder than ever before, and the losses show little sign of stopping anytime soon. candidates.raw_excerpt: Image: This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us. MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand. The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing , in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity. candidates.title: Next Crewed Boeing Starliner Flight Not Until 2028
candidates.raw_excerpt: Two years after Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft landed in the New Mexico desert without NASA’s Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, Boeing and NASA said today it will not be ready to fly astronauts again until 2028. An uncrewed flight test is expected no sooner than the end of this year, but they want another year or more to evaluate those results before putting people aboard. One clear message from the NASA-Boeing news conference at Kennedy Space Center is that both remain committed to Starliner despite persistent problems since the first test flight in 2019. L-R: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Program Manager Dana Weigel, NASA astronaut Woody Hoburg, and Boeing Vice President and Program Manager for Commercial Crew John Mulholland. Screenshot from NASA news conference September 28, 2026. In 2014 , NASA awarded fixed-price contracts to Boeing and SpaceX to design, build, and launch “commercial crew” spacecraft to restore America’s ability to send astronauts to the International Space Station. From 2011 when the Space Shuttle was terminated until SpaceX’s Crew Dragon made its first flight in 2020, NASA had to pay Russia for crew transportation services at a price that ultimately reached $90 million per seat. From the beginning NASA wanted two commercial crew providers to ensure redundancy and competition. That remains the goal today, but SpaceX is the only one because of Starliner’s repeated technical failures. SpaceX’s 13th operational flight is getting ready to launch later this week. China plans to complete a new-generation geological map of Mars by the end of 2028, according to Hou Zengqian, chief scientist of the Tianwen-3 mission, who's an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The new map will propose a Chinese approach to the geological timescale of Mars and seek to promote the geological chronology standard independently developed by China as a globally recognized framework, Hou said.

The map will incorporate the latest scientific findings from China's exploration of Mars. Data from the Zhurong rover indicate that an intercontinental-scale ancient ocean may have existed on Mars about 3.5 billion years ago, while a short-lived flooding event may have occurred around 1.6 billion years ago.

The new-generation geological map of Mars will also include 1:50,000-scale geological maps of landing sites, to be compiled on a corresponding schedule, as well as a series of specialized map collections.

These achievements will serve as a key outcome of the scientific preparation for the Tianwen-3 mission. The results will be released as the world's first intelligent geological map of Mars, according to reports.

The project is also expected to provide a research paradigm and implementation template for future geological mapping missions involving the moon, Venus and asteroids.

Scientists have created a bizarre form of ice that is hotter than lava yet remains solid – a material that may help explain why Uranus and Neptune have such strange magnetic fields.

The material is called superionic ice. It is not like the ice in your freezer. Under extreme pressure and heat, water can enter a strange state in which oxygen atoms form a solid framework while hydrogen nuclei move through it like a liquid. That makes the ice electrically conductive.

The researchers found that the oxygen atoms settled into a previously unknown crystal structure, a discovery that helps explain how this exotic ice behaves.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: RAF The United Kingdom has established a new specialised unit within the Royal Air Force to counter hostile threats to the country’s satellites. The Ministry of Defence announced the formation of No. III Space Effects Squadron on 23 September, describing it as the UK’s first unit dedicated to “disrupting, degrade, and deny hostile threats in space.” The new unit is part of the RAF’s broader plans to build out capabilities for what Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth described as “orbital warfare” during his keynote address at the UK Space Power Conference. “To help our nation fulfil the control of space requirement, UK defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare,” Smyth said. According to Smyth, No. III Space Effects Squadron will be staffed by specialist personnel from across the British armed forces and will support both offensive and defensive space operations. He explained that this would include electronic warfare and capabilities to counter anti-satellite weapons. “These capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.” Exactly what systems No. III Space Effects Squadron will operate remains unclear. European Spaceflight asked the Ministry of Defence whether No. III Space Effects Squadron would operate the UK’s existing ground-based satellite-jamming capability and whether it could provide additional details about the “orbital warfare” capabilities Smyth said were under development. In both cases, a Ministry of Defence spokesperson declined to share any information, saying it was classified. Three More Space Squadrons Planned The RAF already operates No. I Space Operations Squadron as part of the National Space Operations Centre and No. II Space Warning Squadron, which conducts operations from RAF Fylingdales.
